question: How should a neural turbulence closure be trained inside a differentiable coarse solver so that it remains stable and accurate over long rollouts rather than matching one-step DNS targets only?

key_findings.claim: The closure is optimized a posteriori through an unrolled PISO fluid solver, so its forcing is judged by the future coarse trajectory it actually induces.
key_findings.evidence: A convolutional network predicts a subgrid forcing field at each solver step. Automatic differentiation propagates velocity-, vorticity-, strain-, spectral-, or turbulence-statistic losses backward through multiple finite-volume/PISO steps, exposing numerical-solver interactions absent from supervised stress fitting.

key_findings.claim: Longer optimization horizons substantially improve rollout stability and long-time statistics up to a problem-dependent saturation point.
key_findings.evidence: On decaying turbulence, temporal mixing layers, and a statistically steady spatial mixing layer, 10–60-step models outperform one-step/supervised closures in later-time MSE, spectra, momentum thickness, and Reynolds stresses. Very long horizons yield diminishing benefit and diffuse gradients.

key_findings.claim: Loss choice controls which physical statistics are recovered; matching the resolved field alone does not guarantee the right energy transfer.
key_findings.evidence: The paper compares direct L2 with turbulence, strain-rate, spectral, and combined losses. Energy spectra and network work analyses show some low-MSE models inject/dissipate energy incorrectly, while physics-informed terms improve selected statistics and long-time behavior.

key_findings.claim: Stable extrapolation beyond the training horizon is demonstrated in three two-dimensional regular-grid flows, but scaling to three-dimensional industrial CFD is unresolved.
key_findings.evidence: Reported learned simulations remain stable for far more steps than were differentiated and can be up to roughly fourteen times faster than comparably accurate fine-grid solvers. Memory grows with unroll length; all main cases use 2D Cartesian grids, a compact CNN, and expensive DNS-derived targets.

method.core_idea: Train a neural subgrid closure on the coarse solver's own multi-step dynamics and physical statistics, not an offline pointwise surrogate target.
method.mechanism: Downsampled DNS states initialize a finite-volume PISO solver. At each step a CNN supplies closure forcing; the solver advances while preserving numerical constraints. Several future steps are unrolled, trajectory/statistic losses are accumulated, and adjoint/autodiff gradients update the CNN. Horizon and truncated-gradient variants control cost.
assumptions: The differentiable PISO implementation faithfully represents deployment numerics.
DNS trajectories and downsampling define a physically appropriate target coarse dynamics.
Two-dimensional test flows capture key stability mechanisms of turbulent closure learning.
The selected finite horizon is long enough to expose instability but short enough for useful gradients and memory.

techniques.role: Carries closure effects through pressure correction and future states.
Parameterizes unresolved turbulence influence on the coarse velocity field.
Optimizes a posteriori trajectory behavior and mitigates deployment distribution shift.
Targets strain, energy spectra, turbulent kinetic energy, and flow thickness beyond pointwise MSE.
Trades gradient relevance against memory and vanishing/diffuse long-horizon signal.

evaluations.metric: Velocity MSE, resolved kinetic-energy spectra, stability, and closure work at early/late times.
evaluations.result: Multi-step differentiable models track DNS spectra and remain stable much longer than one-step supervised/no-model baselines; a 30-step setting is especially strong in reported comparisons.
evaluations.baseline: No closure, classical LES, supervised one-step CNN, and shorter-horizon differentiable models.

evaluations.setting: Temporal mixing layer with varying horizon and turbulence losses.
evaluations.metric: Late-time field MSE, vorticity, energy spectra, and momentum thickness.
evaluations.result: Ten- and thirty-step physics-aware models greatly reduce late error; longer horizons improve far rollout until returns saturate.
evaluations.baseline: No-model solver, one-step/supervised training, and alternate horizon/loss combinations.

evaluations.setting: Statistically steady spatial mixing layer and gradient truncation studies.
evaluations.metric: Long-run stability, downstream vorticity thickness, Reynolds statistics, and training cost.
evaluations.result: Long-horizon closures remain stable and reproduce key statistics; truncated gradients retain much benefit at lower memory than full very-long unrolling.
evaluations.baseline: No closure and shorter/full versus truncated horizon variants.

limitations: Main demonstrations are two-dimensional on regular Cartesian meshes, not three-dimensional wall-bounded industrial turbulence.
Differentiating long solver trajectories is memory- and compute-intensive and requires an editable differentiable solver.
Training targets depend on expensive DNS and a particular filter/downsampling/discretization.
Generalization to new Reynolds numbers, geometries, grids, and numerical schemes is limited.
A learned stable rollout has no formal conservation or stability guarantee.
failure_modes: One-step supervised closures can be accurate off-solver yet destabilize the coupled rollout.
Long unrolls can produce vanishing, exploding, or temporally diffuse gradients.
A pointwise loss can reward visually close fields while learning the wrong energy transfer.
Changing discretization changes the implicit filter and can invalidate the learned forcing.
reusable_insights: Validate learned dynamics a posteriori inside the deployment solver and far beyond the training horizon.
Optimization horizon is a core modeling hyperparameter, not just a memory setting.
Use physical-statistic losses and energy-budget audits alongside field MSE.
Truncated long-horizon gradients can capture solver interaction without storing the full rollout.
open_questions: Can adjoint/checkpointing or surrogate sensitivities make solver-aware training practical in 3D?
How can closures generalize across discretizations, meshes, Reynolds numbers, and geometries?
What stability and conservation constraints can be imposed without blocking needed backscatter?

competitive_landscape.title: Differentiable Turbulence: Closure as a partial differential equation constrained optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: Formulates turbulence-closure learning explicitly as PDE-constrained optimization through differentiable simulation.
competitive_landscape.difference: It develops a broader optimization formulation; this paper provides detailed horizon/loss studies in a differentiable PISO solver across three 2D flows.

competitive_landscape.title: End-to-end differentiable learning of turbulence models from indirect observations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Learns turbulence models through differentiable RANS/flow solvers using indirect observable losses.
competitive_landscape.difference: It emphasizes inference from indirect observations in a RANS setting; this work emphasizes LES-like subgrid forcing, physical losses, and multi-step horizon stability.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning of Solver-Aware Turbulence Closures from Nudged LES Dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Targets solver-aware stable closures and discretization generalization using nudged LES trajectories.
competitive_landscape.difference: It avoids differentiating/modifying the LES solver and conditions on numerical scheme, directly addressing the cost and solver-specificity of unrolled differentiable training.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Embedding the closure in a differentiable PISO solver and optimizing multi-step physics-based losses produces stable, accurate learned turbulence models with a controllable optimal horizon.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Three flows, extensive horizon/loss ablations, long extrapolative rollouts, physical spectra/statistics, and supervised comparisons support the claim in 2D.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The horizon study and physical diagnostics are unusually thorough; differentiable-solver cost and discretization specificity remain decisive barriers to broad CFD use.
